short: The Anglo-American heavy tank meant to win 1919, finished too late for any war.
full:
The Mark VIII, called the Liberty or International, was to be built in thousands for the campaign planned for 1919: British hulls and armament, an American 300 hp Liberty aero engine, and final assembly at a purpose-built plant at Neuvy-Pailloux in France. Albert Stern's scheme was ratified by the Foreign Secretary, Arthur Balfour, and the American ambassador, Walter Hines Page, on 19 January 1918. The design was the last of the rhomboids and the best of them: engine separated from the crew by a bulkhead, 12-cylinder power, and a trench-crossing span no earlier tank matched.

The armistice came first. Seven were built in Britain, and another twenty-four assembled afterwards from parts already made; the French factory never opened. The United States completed 100 at Rock Island Arsenal in 1919 and 1920, and they equipped the 67th Infantry (Tank) at Aberdeen, Maryland, as America's only heavy tanks between the wars. Phased out from 1932, all were in storage by 1934, and most were passed to Canada in 1940 as training vehicles.
